newsitem.title: INDIA: Hindu convert picked to succeed Mother Teresa.
newsitem.headline: Hindu convert picked to succeed Mother Teresa.

text.p: A former Hindu who converted to Roman Catholicism has been elected to succeed ailing Mother Teresa as the leader of her religious order, the office of the archbishop of Calcutta said on Thursday.
"Sister Nirmala, M.C. (Missionaries of Charity) was elected almost unanimously as the new Superior General," Archbishop Henry D'Souza's office said in a statement released in the eastern Indian city.
"Mother Teresa was present for the election and blessed Sister Nirmala," it said.
Mother Teresa, suffering from heart, kidney and lung ailments, had said she did not want to continue to lead the Missionaries of Charity order that she founded in 1948.
Sister Nirmala, 63, was born into a Nepali Brahmin family and later converted to Roman Catholicism.

She has supervised the order's centres in Europe and the United States. More recently, Sister Nirmala has headed the order's contemplative wing, in which elite nuns dedicate their lives to meditation.
She was not one of the order's councillors-general and thus was considered a dark horse in the eight-week election process.
The election of Mother Teresa's successor had been postponed twice since September. It was first set for September 8, but put off because Mother Teresa was ill.
More than 100 nuns from around the world then went into retreat on January 16 and had planned to vote in a secret ballot on February 2.
But the order's electoral college, apparently unable to find a clear-cut successor, decided instead to hold closed-door deliberations before taking a vote.
Roman Catholic rules stipulate that the superior general of any order can be elected for a maximum of six years and re-elected for one more term.

But successive popes made an exception for Mother Teresa, who founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1948 in the eastern Indian city of Calcutta. In past elections, Mother Teresa has won all the votes -- except her own.
This time she had asked to step down due to poor health.
Any sister of the order who had completed at least five years after her final vows was eligible to run.
Three councillors-general -- sisters Frederick, Joseph Michael and Priscilla Lewis -- had been considered the front-runners.
The Vatican had no direct influence on the vote, but it must ratify the final choice. The election process involved the 132 members of the order's electoral order, or the General Chapter.
Mother Teresa never groomed a successor. Her successor was expected to try to make up in administrative ability what she may lack in charisma compared to the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner.
